analysis.one_liner: Requires private health insurance to cover hearing implant devices, related care, and periodic device upgrades.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was introduced with a Republican lead sponsor and 8 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the Senate health committee in March 2023, and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Ally's Act would require group and individual health plans to cover auditory implant devices — including bone-conduction and cochlear implants — plus their maintenance, repair, upgrades every five years, surgery, hearing assessments, and rehabilitation services. Plans could not charge extra cost-sharing for these items, impose special limits, or deny coverage based on their own review of medical necessity. The bill applied to plan years starting in 2025, but it was never considered by the Senate committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: People with hearing loss who qualify for auditory implant devices, and their families. Many private plans exclude or sharply limit coverage of these devices, which can cost tens of thousands of dollars out of pocket; the bill would force coverage on the same financial terms as other medical benefits, and would bar insurers from overriding a physician's or audiologist's determination that a patient qualifies.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and group or individual insurance to cover auditory implant devices (including bone-conduction and cochlear implants), external sound processors, their maintenance, repair, and an upgrade or replacement every five years, plus assessments, surgery, post-operative visits, and aural rehabilitation services.

Bars plans from applying cost-sharing or treatment limits to these items that are more restrictive than what they apply to other medical and surgical benefits, and from creating separate cost-sharing or limits just for these items.

Prohibits plans and insurers from denying or limiting coverage of any covered item or service based on the plan's own review of medical necessity, leaving the qualification decision to a physician or qualified audiologist.

Closes a loophole so the mandate applies even to grandfathered health plans — plans that are otherwise exempt from many new coverage requirements — and takes effect for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2025.

Applies to employer plans under ERISA and the Internal Revenue Code as well as to insurance regulated under the Public Health Service Act, so the protection reaches workers in self-insured employer plans too.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that fund health plans bear the added cost of covering devices and services they currently exclude or limit, likely passed along in premiums. Hearing device manufacturers gain a mandated customer base at public-subsidized prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, employers, and all premium payers

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises premiums: coverage for expensive implant systems, their maintenance and five-year replacement cycles, and a ban on medical-necessity review all add costs that insurers and employer plans would spread across all enrollees, including people who never need these devices.

Eliminating medical-necessity review entirely — rather than requiring a reasonable review process — removes an insurer check on whether a specific implant or upgrade is clinically appropriate, which some plans argue invites overuse or supplier-driven demand.

The bill is a one-size-fits-all federal mandate on all group and individual plans, including plans in states that have chosen different benefit rules, which overrides state-level decisions about what insurance must cover.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the relatively small population whose doctors determine they need auditory implants, the benefit is large: these devices can cost tens of thousands of dollars, and many plans currently deny or bury the cost. The costs — higher premiums spread across all insured people and the removal of insurer necessity review — are real but diffuse, and comparable to the tradeoffs in other federal insurance mandates (mental health parity, contraception coverage). The bill's chief design weakness is the total ban on medical-necessity review, which goes further than most benefit mandates. On balance it is a consumer-protection mandate whose costs are broad and shallow and whose benefits are deep and concentrated.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee never took the bill up after referring it on March 30, 2023, and the bill died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Shelley Moore Capito introduced Ally's Act on March 30, 2023, with Senators Elizabeth Warren and John Hickenlooper, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
Eight Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill, making it a bipartisan effort led by a Republican with Democratic support.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup and the full Senate never voted, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors are better off because the bill died — they continue to be able to exclude or limit coverage of hearing implant devices and to deny claims through their own necessity reviews. People who need these devices and their families are left to pay out of pocket or fight plan denials.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican lead sponsor (Capito) with Democratic support — original cosponsors Warren and Hickenlooper plus 8 of 48 Senate Democrats as cosponsors — and no recorded opposition ever appeared, because it never advanced past committee.

industries.note: The bill forces insurers to cover hearing implant devices, related care, and five-year upgrades on the same terms as other medical benefits, and strips their ability to deny these claims through their own medical-necessity reviews. Insurers opposed bearing this new coverage obligation.

Employers that fund group plans would pay for the added benefit, likely through higher premiums. The requirement also applies to self-insured ERISA plans, which are normally exempt from state benefit mandates.

The mandate guarantees a paying customer base for bone-conduction and cochlear implant systems, sound processors, and five-year upgrades, with no insurer medical-necessity gatekeeping. Patients benefit from coverage of devices they need, and manufacturers gain a locked-in revenue stream.

industries.industry: Audiologists, implant surgeons, and hearing rehabilitation providers
industries.note: The bill guarantees coverage of assessments, surgery, post-operative care, and aural rehabilitation services, expanding the demand and reimbursement for hearing care providers.
